paper.title: ProgPrompt: Generating Situated Robot Task Plans using Large Language Models
paper.central_claim: A programmatic (Pythonic) LLM prompt structure - imported action primitives, a list of environment objects, example programs with natural-language comments and assert-based state checks with recovery actions - lets an LLM generate executable, situated task plans that work across environments, robot capabilities and tasks; the authors claim state-of-the-art success on VirtualHome household tasks and deployment on a physical robot arm for tabletop tasks.
paper.scope_note: In scope (LLM planner controlling a simulated household agent and a real Franka arm). GPT-3/Codex era; treated as frontier LLM of its time.

evidence.quote: We present a programmatic LLM prompt structure that enables plan generation functional across situated environments, robot capabilities, and tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Author central claim and its stated scope.

evidence.quote: such methods either require enumerating all possible next steps for scoring, or generate free-form text that may contain actions not possible on a given robot in its current context
evidence.support_explanation: Author-stated gap: scoring needs enumeration; free-form generation may be non-executable.

evidence.quote: InnerMonologue [ 1 ] introduces environment feedback and state monitoring, but still found that LLM planners proposed actions involving objects not present in the scene.
evidence.support_explanation: Nearest neighbour with environment feedback and the residue it leaves.

evidence.quote: The entire plan is generated open-loop without any environment interaction , and later tested for executability of matched actions.
evidence.support_explanation: Closest ancestor (Huang et al. [2]) is open-loop with post-hoc action matching.

evidence.quote: SayCan constructs a set of all admissible actions expressed in natural language and scores them using an LLM.
evidence.support_explanation: SayCan neighbour: enumerate-and-score, hard for combinatorial action spaces.

evidence.quote: Concurrent with our work are Socratic models [ 3 ] , which also use code-completion to generate robot plans.
evidence.support_explanation: Concurrent code-completion planner; not compared empirically.

evidence.quote: These encourage the LLM to restrict its output to only functions that are available in the current context.
evidence.support_explanation: Imports soften (not enforce) the action vocabulary; no decoding constraint.

evidence.quote: We provide the available objects in the environment as a list of strings.
evidence.support_explanation: Object-list channel (global list in VirtualHome).

evidence.quote: Assertions provide an environment feedback mechanism to make sure that the preconditions hold, and enable error recovery when they do not.
evidence.support_explanation: Assert-and-recover operation.

evidence.quote: we extract information about the relevant object from the state graph and prompt the LLM to return whether the assertion holds or not given the state graph and assertion as a text prompt
evidence.support_explanation: Assertions are judged by an LLM over a symbolic state graph; the checker is not an external sound checker and is not audited.

evidence.quote: SR is the fraction of executions that achieved all task-relevant goal-conditions.
evidence.support_explanation: Success is decided by simulator goal conditions against one recorded final state.

evidence.quote: Each result is averaged over 5 runs in a single VH environment across 10 tasks.
evidence.support_explanation: Denominator and scope of the main table: one scene, 10 tasks, 5 runs.

evidence.quote: Baseline from Huang et al. [ 2 ] GPT3 0.00 \pm 0.00 0.45 \pm 0.03 0.21 \pm 0.03
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline [2] SR 0.00 / Exec 0.45 / GCR 0.21; compare ProgPrompt GPT3 SR 0.34 / Exec 0.84 / GCR 0.65 (row 3).

evidence.quote: [ 2 ] use 1 dynamically selected example, as described in their paper.
evidence.support_explanation: Baseline gets 1 example versus 3 fixed examples for ProgPrompt: unequal prompt budget.
Full GPT3 ProgPrompt row; rows 4-6 (feedback / comments toggled) give SR 0.28+-0.04, 0.30+-0.00, 0.18+-0.04 - some gaps are within 1-2 sd.

evidence.quote: Second, we observe that removing Comments from the prompt code substantially reduces performance on all metrics
evidence.support_explanation: Comment ablation claim (toggle, backbone fixed).

evidence.quote: because some tasks have multiple appropriate goal states
evidence.support_explanation: Authors concede that single-final-state scoring mislabels valid alternative goal states (measurement noise, uncharacterised).

evidence.locator: Sec V-A Other Environments / Table III
evidence.quote: We evaluate on 10 tasks each in two additional VH scenes beyond scene Env-0 where other reported results take place.
evidence.support_explanation: Scene holdout: Env-1/Env-2 SR 0.56 each; no baseline run there.

evidence.quote: We include 3 Pythonic task plan examples per prompt after evaluating performance on VH for between 1 prompt and 7 prompts
evidence.support_explanation: Prompt design choice made by evaluating on the same VirtualHome setting that is reported (development overlap).

evidence.quote: Thus, we finetune GPT2 to learn a policy
evidence.support_explanation: The LangPrompt baseline needs an extra trained GPT2 action-mapper, so it differs from ProgPrompt in more than prompt format.

evidence.quote: Therefore, we intend the physical results to serve as a qualitative demonstration of the ease with which our prompting approach allows constraining and grounding LLM-generated plans to a physical robot system.
evidence.support_explanation: Authors label the real-robot evidence qualitative.

evidence.quote: Due to real world uncertainty, we do not implement assert -based closed loop options on the tabletop plans.
evidence.support_explanation: Assertion feedback (a core component) is not exercised on the real robot.

evidence.quote: We report an additional metric Plan SR , which refers to whether the plan would have likely succeeded , provided successful pick-and-place execution without gripper failures.
evidence.support_explanation: Real-robot Plan SR is a counterfactual, not an executed success; Table IV lists 9 single-run rows (SR succeeded 7/9, Plan SR 8/9).

evidence.quote: Action success feedback is not provided to the agent, which may lead to failure of the subsequent actions.
evidence.support_explanation: Author-conceded failure mode: no action-success channel.

evidence.quote: However, Codex has limited access in terms of number of queries per minute, so we continue to use GPT3 as our main LLM backbone in the following ablation experiments.
evidence.support_explanation: Only a rate-limit remark; no call/token/latency cost is reported anywhere in the pinned text.

evidence.quote: We use ViLD [ 39 ] , an open-vocabulary object detection model, to identify and segment objects in the scene and construct the available object list for the prompt.
evidence.support_explanation: Real-robot object list comes from a detector, versus a simulator-provided global list in VirtualHome.

evidence.quote: Our method is intuitive and flexible, and generalizes widely to new scenes, agents and tasks, including a real-robot deployment.
evidence.support_explanation: Broad generalisation claim beyond what Tables III-IV test.

signatures.object: The planner prompt: Pythonic header with imported action primitives, an environment object list, three fixed example plan programs with NL comments; the LLM (GPT-3 / Codex / Davinci) completes the next task function.
signatures.information: Sees the action list, the object list (global list of all VirtualHome object instances in the scene; detector output on the real robot) and example programs; does not see the goal state or any state feedback while generating.
signatures.operation: Few-shot code completion of a plan program (API calls over objects plus comments), interpreted step by step by the simulator / robot.
signatures.output: Executable plan function; Exec = share of actions executable.
signatures.conditions: Same primitives as imported; 3 fixed examples (2 for Davinci); object list local per plan on the robot.
signatures.selection_rule: not_applicable: single sampled program per task; backbone (GPT3 vs Codex vs Davinci) and example count compared on the same reported setting.
signatures.persistence: not_applicable: no state kept between tasks; no retained improvement claimed.
signatures.claimed_effect: VirtualHome SR 0.34 / Exec 0.84 / GCR 0.65 (GPT3) vs 0.00 / 0.45 / 0.21 for the re-implemented baseline of [2].
signatures.failure_boundary: Scene-agnostic prompt; environment artifacts; plans cut by API caps; ambiguous tasks; single final-state scoring.

signatures.object: Execution-time assert statements with LLM-judged state checks and recovery actions embedded in the generated program.
signatures.information: VirtualHome state graph (symbolic, object properties and relations) passed to an LLM that answers whether the assertion holds; unavailable on the real robot.
signatures.operation: Before an action, check a precondition; if false run the recovery branch (e.g. find) already written in the plan.
signatures.output: Closed-loop corrected execution inside the plan program.
signatures.conditions: Only simulation; recovery branches must be anticipated by the LLM; no general action-success feedback.
signatures.feedback: LLM judgement of assertion over symbolic state
signatures.claimed_effect: Feedback ablation (rows 3 vs 4, 5 vs 6) improves metrics; SR 0.34 vs 0.28 with comments, 0.30 vs 0.18 without.
signatures.failure_boundary: Generated assertions do not cover all cases; assertion judge is an unaudited LLM.

gap.author_gap: Scoring-style LLM planners need all next steps enumerated; text-generation planners emit actions/objects that do not map to the robot or scene; environment state feedback is missing in LLM task planning.
gap.checked_gap: Real and sourced: the cited neighbours (Huang et al. [2] open-loop with action matching; SayCan enumerate-and-score; InnerMonologue feedback but off-scene objects) each leave the stated residue. Importance for the embodied setting is plausible but only quantified against one neighbour.
lineage: Huang et al. zero-shot planners [2] (open-loop, 1 retrieved example) -> SayCan [4] (affordance-weighted scoring) / InnerMonologue [1] (feedback, still off-scene objects) -> concurrent Socratic Models [3] (code completion) -> ProgPrompt (imports + object list + comments + asserts)
gap.closest_adjacent: InnerMonologue and Socratic Models are the closest (feedback, code completion) but are not empirically compared; only [2] is re-implemented.
gap.residue: Plans that name unavailable actions/objects and never check preconditions against the current state.
gap.stakes: Executability on a given robot and scene (Exec 0.45 for the baseline).
gap.method_response: Pythonic imports and object list narrow the output space; example programs show structure; comments act as chain-of-thought; assertions check preconditions with recovery.
gap.remaining_gap: Strict-goal scoring, ambiguous tasks, no action-success feedback, scene-specific affordances, asserts not exercised on the robot, SR still 0.34.
gap.current_relevance: Later work 2302.01560 (same batch) re-implements ProgPrompt in Minecraft and reports an average success of 16.88 vs 15.42 for a plain zero-shot planner (author re-implementation), suggesting the program format alone transfers weakly to long-horizon open worlds; not used to lower the score.
unresolved: No quantitative comparison with SayCan, InnerMonologue or Socratic Models; closest-neighbour judgement rests on the paper's own related-work text and local pinned sources only.

rs_pattern.reason: Operation maps to adapt_via_conditioning with a secondary executable-artifact/interpreter operation.

executes_pattern.reason: Executes the conditioning schema; the delegation loop is weak because the state check is LLM-judged and absent on the robot.

resolves_problem.reason: Exec 0.84-0.90 vs 0.45 baseline shows far fewer inadmissible actions, but SR 0.34 and Exec<1 leave the executability/situatedness gap open; no evidence of closing it across scenes against strong baselines.

condition_checks.note: Action vocabulary imported into the prompt and executed by the VirtualHome interpreter, but only softly constrained (Exec 0.84, not 1.0).
Action-success feedback is not returned to the model between steps.
Imports and object list are not ablated separately; only comments and asserts are toggled.
No matched call-budget comparison with a non-code planner; one-shot plan generation.
Program format, comments, state checks and interpreter loop are not isolated beyond comments/asserts; the language baseline has a different mapper.
Real-robot evidence is authored as qualitative.

unassigned: LLM-judged precondition assertion over a symbolic state graph with in-plan recovery branches (closest K201, which requires a checker outside the LLM).
revision_proposals: Pending, not applied: note in K201/K105 boundary text that an LLM-judged assert over a state graph is a distinct, weaker variant from a rule-based external checker (single-paper observation, 2209.11302).

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: A unified Pythonic prompt schema (imports + object list + examples) conditions a frozen LLM to emit only primitives of the target agent; changing the agent only needs a new import list.
pattern_mapping.conditions_and_differences: K104 expects a fixed vocabulary executed by a reliable deterministic/frozen executor; here the vocabulary is only prompt-level, executor is the simulator interpreter, and out-of-vocabulary actions still occur (Exec 0.84).

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: The LLM writes an executable program composed of primitives with local branch/recovery that an interpreter runs against the environment.
pattern_mapping.conditions_and_differences: K105 assumes a coding runtime with persistent helpers and requested-only observations; ProgPrompt plans are mostly straight-line one-shot programs with an LLM-judged check, so the match is structural only.

claims.text: Program-style prompts produce executable plans that beat a natural-language baseline on VirtualHome.
claims.setting: VirtualHome Env-0, 10 tasks x 5 runs (50 executions) per row, GPT3 backbone
claims.baseline_control: Re-implemented Huang et al. [2] (1 dynamic example) and LangPrompt (3 NL examples + finetuned GPT2 mapper)
claims.selection_vs_test: Example count, backbone and recipe chosen on the same VirtualHome setting that is reported.
claims.result_denominator: ProgPrompt GPT3 SR 0.34+-0.08, Exec 0.84, GCR 0.65 vs [2] SR 0.00, Exec 0.45, GCR 0.21; 50 executions each.
claims.allowed_conclusion: In one scene and 10 tasks, the program prompt clearly exceeds a re-implemented open-loop baseline; it does not establish state of the art over SayCan/InnerMonologue.

claims.text: Comments and assert/recovery feedback each improve planning.
claims.baseline_control: toggled variants with the same backbone
claims.result_denominator: SR 0.34/0.28/0.30/0.18 for comments+feedback / comments only / feedback only / neither; 5 runs.
counterevidence: Exec is higher without feedback when comments are absent
claims.allowed_conclusion: Comments help consistently; assertion benefit is directionally positive but not resolved statistically.

claims.text: The method generalises to new scenes.
claims.setting: VirtualHome Env-1, Env-2, 10 tasks x 5 runs each
claims.allowed_conclusion: Absolute success is retained on two further scenes with the same primitives; no comparison shows the margin over baselines is retained.

claims.text: The approach deploys on a physical robot arm.
claims.setting: Franka Panda, pick-and-place primitive, ViLD object list, 4 tasks, 9 single-run rows
counterevidence: gripper slip and soup-can/bottle confusion failures
claims.allowed_conclusion: A feasibility demonstration of text-to-plan grounding on one arm with a given pick-and-place policy; not a measured success rate.

assessment.evidence_level_reason: Closed-loop execution in two embodiments (VirtualHome agent and a real Franka arm) with per-run counts, so the EVIDENCE transfer letter is met, but only 9 single-run robot rows, authors call it qualitative and the assert component is not used there; borderline, Opus to confirm.
assessment.strongest_supported_claim: A three-example Pythonic prompt with comments and asserts lets GPT-3/Codex produce far more executable plans than a re-implemented open-loop language baseline in VirtualHome (SR 0.34 vs 0.00 on 10 tasks in one scene) and the format drives a real arm for simple pick-and-place; broad generalisation and state-of-the-art claims over other LLM planners are not supported.
unresolved: contamination of GPT-3/Codex with VirtualHome-style programs
comparison with SayCan / InnerMonologue / Socratic Models
assessment.reproduction: author_report only; no reproduction by us

G.reason: Gap (enumeration cost, non-executable free text, missing state feedback) is specific and tied to named neighbours, and the remaining gaps are listed in V-B. Not 4: only the open-loop baseline [2] is quantitatively compared; SayCan/InnerMonologue/Socratic are described but not run.

M.reason: Import list and object list narrow the output space, comments act as chain-of-thought, asserts check preconditions: a reconstructable, testable mechanism with comment/feedback toggles. Weak points: the language baseline needs an extra learned mapper, assertions are judged by an unaudited LLM, imports/object list never toggled.

X.reason: Prompt construction (III-B), interpreter execution and assertion flow can be rebuilt, and failure boundaries are discussed (V-B). Not 4: LLM-judge prompt details, how recovery branches arise, and why Exec stays below 1 are thin, and the real robot omits the feedback component and uses a different object-list scope.

measurement.reason: Simulator goal conditions with defined SR/Exec/GCR and a clear 50-execution denominator, but only 10 test tasks of the 70-task set are reported without stated reason, single-final-state scoring mislabels valid alternatives (conceded), and the real-robot column is a counterfactual Plan SR with 9 single-run rows. Anchor v2: judgement exists but denominators/validator have gaps -> 2.

causality.reason: Comments/feedback toggled with the backbone fixed and three backbones compared; key confounds remain: baseline gets 1 vs 3 examples and a trained mapper, imports/object list never toggled, and some ablation gaps lie within 1-2 sd.

holdout.reason: Prompt design and backbone were selected on the same VirtualHome setting that is reported; two extra scenes (SR 0.56) and a real arm give some holdout, but there is no baseline in those, 8-9 robot rows, no contamination check. Not 3-4: gain retention over baselines not shown.

statistics.reason: 5 repeats with mean+-sd, per-task table with sd, but sd reflects LLM sampling over a fixed 10-task set, no CI or paired test, and failures are discussed qualitatively not counted.

cost.reason: No LLM call counts, tokens, latency or dollar cost; asserts add LLM calls that are uncounted; the only remark is a Codex rate limit. Backbone is matched with the baseline but prompt example counts are not (3 vs 1).
